section_summary: This section follows American objections to Japan’s proposed automobile industry law under the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, alongside Japanese officials’ differing interpretation of the treaty. It records the law’s passage in May 1936, its likely effects on Ford and General Motors in Japan, and the law and enforcement ordinances as translated by the American Embassy. Departmental notes also examine the ownership of the two American companies’ Japanese subsidiaries.

subfiles.title: Departmental comment on proposed automobile legislation
subfiles.about: The Department assesses Neville’s treaty discussion with the Japanese Vice Minister.
subfiles.summary: The writer recommends further informal discussions asserting American rights under the 1911 treaty, despite a likely delay in legislation following dissolution of the Diet.

subfiles.title: Proposed legislation for controlling the motor car industry in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards a memorandum of Neville’s discussion with the Vice Minister.
subfiles.summary: The Vice Minister was surprised by the American treaty objection, lacked a draft law, and promised to investigate. Grew reports his personal dislike of the proposal.

subfiles.title: Conversation on proposed automobile law
subfiles.about: Neville explains the American treaty objection to Shigemitsu.
subfiles.summary: Neville argues that restrictions on assembly and manufacture would discriminate against American automobile traders. Shigemitsu questions whether the treaty protects manufacture, says no draft is available, and expresses personal opposition to the proposal.

subfiles.title: Law To Control Auto Production Ready For Diet
subfiles.about: A newspaper outlines proposed licensing and restrictions on foreign automobile manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: The draft would require government sanction and Japanese voting control while granting licensed firms tax and financing privileges.

subfiles.title: Treaty right to operate manufactories
subfiles.about: The Department states its interpretation of Article I of the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: The treaty’s reference to manufactories gives American citizens equal manufacturing rights in Japan.

subfiles.title: Treaty analysis of proposed automobile legislation
subfiles.about: A memorandum considers treaty protection for American ownership of Japanese corporations.
subfiles.summary: It distinguishes Article I rights of citizens from Article VII rights of U.S. corporations.

subfiles.title: Japanese interpretation of treaty and automobile bill
subfiles.about: Grew reports Shigemitsu’s view that the proposed law would not violate the treaty.
subfiles.summary: Shigemitsu says Article I concerns individuals and Article VII corporations. Though the Foreign Office dislikes the bill, it cannot assert that treaty obligations bar it.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction on treaty rights and automobile manufacture
subfiles.to: American Consul, Shanghai, for Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A draft rejects Japanese arguments limiting treaty protection for American automobile interests.
subfiles.summary: It argues that barring American citizens from controlling Japanese companies that manufacture cars would nullify Article I rights, and authorizes informal discussion with the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Note on ownership of Ford and General Motors in Japan
subfiles.about: Officials consider whether their treaty argument fits the ownership of the American subsidiaries.
subfiles.summary: Metzger advises checking ownership before sending Ward’s draft. A handwritten May 26 addition reports Commerce records showing ownership by the U.S. parent companies.

subfiles.title: Reservations about draft automobile-law instruction
subfiles.about: A memorandum questions the legal basis of a draft instruction to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The writer compares the proposed argument with restrictions on alien participation in Philippine public works and questions whether American corporations can claim treaty rights to establish Japanese companies.

subfiles.title: Decision to hold proposed instruction in reserve
subfiles.about: Hornbeck records approval to withhold the proposed instruction.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Phillips approves holding the proposed instruction in reserve.

subfiles.title: Continuation of reservations about draft automobile-law instruction
subfiles.about: The April 28 memorandum concludes after an intervening May 28 note.
subfiles.summary: The writer calls the draft the Department’s best available argument but still open to question.

subfiles.title: Comment on Ward’s draft treaty argument
subfiles.about: A memorandum compares Ward’s argument with a Belgian complaint over Philippine public works.
subfiles.summary: The writer remains unconvinced that treaty rights granted to citizens automatically extend to corporations but accepts Ward’s draft as a legal judgment.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning Japanese automobile control law
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes the Embassy to challenge Japan’s treaty interpretation.
subfiles.summary: The instruction holds that Article I protects Americans’ equal right to own and control Japanese automobile corporations and that Article VII does not govern Japanese corporations operating in Japan.

subfiles.title: Comment on Shigemitsu’s treaty interpretation
subfiles.about: A reviewer urges a prompt response to Shigemitsu’s interpretation despite possible legislative delay.
subfiles.summary: The reviewer summarizes a January conversation and argues that the Department should refute Shigemitsu’s reading of Articles I and VII before enactment, even if the bill may be postponed.

subfiles.title: Automobile Control Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards a conversation concerning the bill’s prospects after dissolution of the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Shigemitsu considers near-term enactment unlikely, while the Embassy will continue watching reports that the measure may reach an extraordinary Diet session.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Shigemitsu on Automobile Control Law
subfiles.about: Shigemitsu explains why he sees little immediate value in further discussion.
subfiles.summary: He says the law is unfinished and the dissolved Diet makes early enactment unlikely.

subfiles.title: Automobile Control Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports Japan’s treaty position and pressures favoring automobile legislation.
subfiles.summary: Shigemitsu says Article I covers individuals while Article VII governs corporations. Grew judges that military and industrial pressure to create a Japanese motor industry makes legislation likely despite Foreign Office objections.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Automobile Control Law
subfiles.about: Shigemitsu sets out the Japanese Government’s informal treaty position.
subfiles.summary: He says the proposed law would reserve licensed manufacture to national corporations without discriminating between individuals. He acknowledges Foreign Office opposition but says it cannot claim the treaty prevents the bill.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch 1693
subfiles.about: The note points to another file for Grew’s report on discriminatory automobile legislation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to file 894.00 P.R./98 and despatch 1693.

subfiles.title: Fragment concerning treaty discussions
subfiles.about: An excerpt recounts Neville’s conversations with the Vice Minister.
subfiles.summary: It contrasts the American assembly-rights argument with Japan’s Articles I and VII interpretation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch 1642
subfiles.about: The note points to another file for a report on proposed automobile-manufacturing controls.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to file 894.00 P.R./97 and despatch 1642.

subfiles.title: Proposed legislation for control of automobile manufacture
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes General Motors’ talks with Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: A proposed manufacturing arrangement had not gained approval from company leaders or the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Passage of automobile industry law
subfiles.about: Grew reports passage of the automobile industry law.
subfiles.summary: The Diet passed the law on May 23; a despatch will follow.

subfiles.title: Comment on despatch 1820
subfiles.about: A reviewer points to the law’s effects on Ford and General Motors.
subfiles.summary: The note highlights Ford’s new factory and stalled General Motors merger talks.

subfiles.title: Automobile Industry Control Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew outlines the proposed law and American companies’ responses.
subfiles.summary: The proposed law would license larger manufacturers under Japanese control, protect domestic production, and cap existing foreign plants near their August 1935 output. Ford proceeds with a Tsurumi factory, while General Motors’ merger negotiations with Nippon Sangyo appear deadlocked.

subfiles.title: Comment on passage of automobile industry law
subfiles.about: A reviewer summarizes the Embassy’s report on the newly passed law.
subfiles.summary: The note emphasizes added authority to raise duties on low-priced imports and says no action is required.

subfiles.title: Automobile Industry Control Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports the law’s passage and analyzes its possible effects on American firms.
subfiles.summary: The bill passed both Diet houses without floor opposition. New powers to restrict imports and raise duties could erode American firms’ existing sales, though the eventual effect depends on enforcement regulations and competing views within the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards an English translation of the promulgated law.
subfiles.summary: The enacted text broadly matches the reported draft and gives the Government powers to inspect companies, fix prices, and direct military production. Its practical effect awaits enforcement regulations.

subfiles.title: Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law
subfiles.about: The Embassy’s translation sets out the enacted automobile manufacturing law.
subfiles.summary: The law establishes licensing, Japanese majority ownership requirements, tax privileges, and government powers over imports, prices, business plans, inspections, and military production. Supplementary rules permit preexisting manufacturers to continue within their earlier scale of business.

subfiles.title: Enforcement date and scope of automobile law
subfiles.about: Grew reports publication of enforcement ordinances.
subfiles.summary: The law takes effect July 11 and applies above 750 cc and 3,000 cars annually.

subfiles.title: Comment on enforcement ordinances
subfiles.about: A reviewer summarizes the Embassy’s report on enforcement rules.
subfiles.summary: The rules apply to production above 3,000 units yearly. Higher duties or quotas remain possible, but the Embassy expects administration to avoid immediate harm to American interests.

subfiles.title: Ownership of General Motors Japan
subfiles.about: Moser relays a Commerce inquiry into General Motors Japan’s capital stock.
subfiles.summary: General Motors Export Corporation reports that General Motors Corporation owns all outstanding stock outright or beneficially.

subfiles.title: Cover letter on Ford Japan stock
subfiles.about: Commerce forwards a reply about Ford Japan’s stock.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses Ford ownership information and promises General Motors information later.

subfiles.title: Ford and General Motors of Japan
subfiles.from: R. L. Whaley, Detroit District Office
subfiles.about: Whaley reports Ford Japan’s share ownership.
subfiles.summary: Ford’s U.S. parent owns 159,994 of 160,000 shares; American citizens hold six.

subfiles.title: Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law enforcement ordinances
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards translations of three ordinances and assesses their immediate effect.
subfiles.summary: The rules set 750 cc and 3,000-car thresholds and establish detailed reporting and exemption procedures. Grew expects possible higher duties or quotas but considers the current regulations relatively liberal for American interests.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 169
subfiles.about: The ordinance fixes the automobile law’s effective date.
subfiles.summary: The law is ordered into force on July 11, 1936.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 170
subfiles.about: The ordinance defines covered vehicles and production and tax-exemption procedures.
subfiles.summary: It sets a 750 cc vehicle threshold and 3,000-vehicle annual production threshold, and prescribes tax and import-duty exemption procedures.

subfiles.title: Regulations for Enforcement of the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law
subfiles.from: Gotarō Ogawa, Minister of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: The ordinance specifies covered parts and application and reporting requirements.
subfiles.summary: It lists regulated automobile parts and the information required for manufacturing licenses, changes in operations, public notices, and import-duty exemption permits. The text continues beyond page 160.
